lxc_5bc4dc9123297e27.text: Markets can jump or fall in a single day, while whole economies and long investment plans usually move more slowly.

lxc_6abbd1088c8b751e.text: These ideas help you see the difference between a short scare and a longer money choice.

lxc_73b71a7eccb0a2b4.text: An economy does not grow at the same speed all the time.

lxc_27ee3448f1a6f4ab.text: A **business cycle** is the longer pattern of growth and slowdown.

lxc_a9aab28a832820f2.text: The **NBER**, a US research group, records these cycles by marking peaks and troughs.

lxc_b20f925272b1bdcb.text: A peak is a high point.

lxc_6bf40d5e8ed5f519.text: A trough is a low point.

lxc_bf13c43297717e83.text: An **expansion** runs from a trough to a peak, as economic activity grows.

lxc_04754739b7d8df41.text: A **recession** runs from a peak to a trough, as activity falls.

lxc_4068ea732b798f70.text: The NBER says expansion is the normal state of the economy, and most recessions are brief.

lxc_9360fb4df98bf2c4.text: The expansion that began in June 2009 and ended in February 2020 lasted 128 months — the longest US expansion in the NBER record back to 1854.

lxc_35eb57656db203f9.text: The COVID recession that followed, from February 2020 to April 2020, lasted only two months — the shortest US recession on that record.

lxc_4b80a88ebae188e5.text: One wild market week is not the same thing as a whole business cycle.

lxc_8a5926d6e9777d99.text: When people talk about timing, it helps to separate daily noise from a wider economic change.

lxc_7186b93c2926a964.text: **Trading** usually means trying to benefit from shorter price moves.

lxc_03c187a3ccaf9f92.text: A trader may buy and sell often, like someone who keeps switching phone plans to catch a short discount.

lxc_51b29abbe0af855a.text: **Investing** usually means owning something for longer, so growth and compounding have time to work — more like planting a tree and waiting for shade.

lxc_7d5e9419c03bf3b6.text: Both traders and investors sell, but their reasons and time periods can be different.

lxc_46f80a7d88d38c17.text: Selling is not the opposite of investing.

lxc_020b2dc33c812937.text: It is one action inside a larger plan.

lxc_944db07a9a870c58.text: The important questions are why you are selling and what happens next.

lxc_35d62ae9b7f65a4e.text: Imagine two neighbours who both own shares in a broad US stock index.

lxc_437bc3894bdeb68e.text: One sells after a few sharp down days, hoping to buy again later at a cheaper price.

lxc_891e20a7f161e816.text: The other keeps a long plan and stays invested through the bounce.

lxc_dc805666364a6dca.text: **Market timing** means trying to buy and sell at perfect moments.

lxc_6e80b9b6e56658ae.text: In practice it needs two successful decisions: leave before a fall, then return before a rise.

lxc_1b9ca039ef60a631.text: The Bank of Singapore explains that most people get one or both of those decisions wrong.

lxc_60f98d71be11263a.text: Here is a real pattern the bank describes.

lxc_fd7a837357925a83.text: A person sells to feel safe.

lxc_2309e6107a164927.text: Then the recovery begins while that person is still waiting for a “clear” signal.

lxc_f920d15397649a68.text: By the time the person feels brave enough to buy again, many of the best rebound days may already have passed.

lxc_e767a37eb81693c4.text: Early 2020 showed how fast that story can move.

lxc_6f8ff9d9b3bf1b4b.text: After the February 2020 peak, the COVID shock hit hard and quickly.

lxc_55ec7e29ca19fc4f.text: Many share prices fell, then recovered over the following months while the short recession was already ending.

lxc_e31cd515820647e9.text: Someone who sold only from fear, and then waited too long, could miss the rebound even if the original worry felt reasonable on the worst day.

lxc_e2676c74adbef3f0.text: Charles Schwab’s research centre studied five imaginary investors to show the cost of waiting for perfection.

lxc_a3729d041adb3868.text: Each person received $2,000 every year for 20 years ending in 2024.

lxc_d395daaf2654f4ab.text: The study tracked the **S&P 500**, an index of large US companies.

lxc_c5954be4f9138b33.text: One investor timed each yearly purchase perfectly and finished near $186,077.

lxc_26bf97079101cc26.text: Another invested on the first trading day of each year and finished near $170,555 — only about $15,522 less.

lxc_18c96972788d39a6.text: Regular fixed investments, on a regular schedule, called **dollar-cost averaging**, finished near $166,591.

lxc_24bac13ec78dfa7b.text: Even the worst yearly timing still beat staying in cash, which ended near $47,357.

lxc_51f9990b7a13a14a.text: Perfect timing won, but ordinary early investing came close.

lxc_1ea648fdac371d58.text: Waiting in cash came last by a wide gap.

lxc_05aaa9c41410e891.text: Across 80 rolling periods of 20 years going back to 1926, investing immediately almost never finished last.

lxc_afc902dd9d131a4b.text: The study does not say coming years will all look the same.

lxc_870c84ffd4deb644.text: It shows why waiting for a perfect entry can be expensive compared with a simple, early plan.

lxc_9ae0c4641d1cee32.text: **Time in the market** means staying invested over long periods instead of repeatedly hunting for perfect buying and selling days.

lxc_4f28b899c3692889.text: That can feel hard during a sharp fall.

lxc_535c35a150a614e4.text: The mechanism matters: strong market days often happen close to very weak ones.

lxc_68763c9ad1acfae0.text: RBC looked at market history back to 1973.

lxc_0dfea83633c568a1.text: Missing only the 10 most profitable trading days cut returns to about half compared with staying invested over that long period.

lxc_91bf131625d6c332.text: A shorter example showed the same timing problem.

lxc_573fa3cb34158aeb.text: In 2023 through August, the S&P 500 was up nearly 18%.

lxc_8d1e723430a4258b.text: An investor who missed the 10 best days had losses instead.

lxc_6a1f140b1aa8e7ce.text: So the danger is not only the fall itself.

lxc_89560091daa1a689.text: If someone sells during fear and holds cash, the recovery may begin before that person feels ready to return.

lxc_f4d8565788d7282a.text: The best days can arrive in a cluster right when the news still feels bad.

lxc_07cad756f1e6cf74.text: **Compounding** happens when earlier growth can produce more growth.

lxc_ffd569b29725266f.text: Interest or gains are added to the original amount, and later growth can build on that larger total.

lxc_aa35f0f2e27e4f75.text: It becomes more powerful as time passes, so time is not only a background detail.

lxc_0354c32880d534cb.text: It is part of how long-term investing works.

lxc_e1401eead7bce5b6.text: The Bank of Singapore used a simple illustration of $100 growing at 8% for 20 years.

lxc_9c7e5ab20e22f585.text: It compared compound growth with simple returns.

lxc_eb6b393fd356abf5.text: At first, the difference was small.

lxc_cc7deb38fc179ce1.text: Later, it grew wider, reaching about $206 by year 20 in the illustration.

lxc_da207074b435ce12.text: The bank also compared $100 in the S&P 500 from 1970 through 2024.

lxc_c87404a2c6ceaf01.text: Staying fully invested produced a very different result from missing the best 1% of weeks.

lxc_8d8a118f56b9bc74.text: This does not make every short fall unimportant.

lxc_87f7d9a316a3df0f.text: It shows why short-term noise is not the whole story.

lxc_0d9915b4fd7f0421.text: Compounding needs time in the market.

lxc_57e176ee9e20764b.text: Market timing that keeps pulling money out can interrupt that process.

lxc_7b36e0f33338872f.text: **Opportunity cost** is the next-best use of money or time that you give up when you choose something.

lxc_14ccff47b75b8621.text: An OpenStax example asks you to imagine that a burger costs the same as four bus tickets.

lxc_3c99bd1e6e4e2f82.text: The real cost of the burger includes the four trips you can no longer take.

lxc_526a84b0c9f90ae7.text: The same lens works for investing.

lxc_bfee0802ea10ba1a.text: Look at the choice, the alternative, and the result.

lxc_38646983fbdf5e73.text: Cash can provide patience and flexibility, but money left outside the market gives up the chance to grow.

lxc_60a5afb55d009d23.text: Selling can remove you from a possible fall, but it can also remove you from a sudden recovery.

lxc_e940ea69a5616d84.text: Waiting for a perfect moment has a cost too.

lxc_f7b4f57cf860a31a.text: The earlier studies do not promise that every investment will rise.

lxc_e27c8eb6d4b2df02.text: They show why “doing nothing yet” is still a decision with a trade-off.

lxc_04db4dfa7ee602f0.text: Business cycles, trading versus investing, market timing, missing best days, and compounding all meet here: each money choice gives up another path.
